title: Multicast and IGMP
text: An exchange feed has hundreds of subscribers, and every one of them wants each packet first. Multicast is how one send reaches all of them.

title: Why multicast
text: With unicast, the exchange sends one copy per subscriber, and the last copy leaves after all the others. With multicast, it sends a single packet to a group address. The network copies it at each branch, so every subscriber gets the same bytes at almost the same moment. The sender's cost does not grow with the audience.

title: Group addresses
text: Group addresses run from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. The 239 block is administratively scoped, meant to stay inside one organisation. On Ethernet, the low 23 bits of the group go into a MAC address starting 01:00:5E. So 239.1.1.1 becomes 01:00:5E:01:01:01. A group has 28 significant bits, so 32 groups share each MAC, and the NIC can pass up traffic you never asked for.

title: IGMP version 3
text: A host joins with IGMP. The kernel sends a Membership Report to 224.0.0.22, with TTL 1, so it never leaves the link. A querier asks again every 125 seconds by default, sending to 224.0.0.1. If no report arrives for 260 seconds, the membership expires. Version 3 also filters by source: in include mode, you take the group only from the senders you list.

title: IGMP snooping
text: A plain switch floods multicast out of every port. A snooping switch reads the IGMP reports passing through it. It then forwards each group only to ports with members, plus the ports that lead to routers. So the feed reaches the servers that joined, and nobody else's link fills up.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's UDP receiver does the join in a few lines. It binds the group address itself, not any address, so other groups on the same port stay out. It asks for a 16 megabyte receive buffer, then adds membership on the chosen interface. The setup script routes 239 slash 8 to loopback, so every lab feed stays inside the machine.

title: Pitfalls
text: Three things bite in production. Join on the wrong interface, and the report goes out of the wrong port. Lose the querier, and snooping switches can age out your port; the feed simply stops. And size receive buffers for the open, because a burst that overflows them is lost before you see it. Multicast is one send to many, and IGMP is the contract that keeps it flowing.
